title: Vesak, the fifth time
hook: one full moon for his birth, awakening and passing
tomorrow: after he woke up, who heard his first sermon, and where?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a life of practice: don't harm, do good, purify the mind. A child can say it; an old man is still doing it. That closed the block: few wants, room to breathe, three jewels, a vow, said aloud. Now the festival year opens.
screen: `A LIFE OF PRACTICE.` → `THE FESTIVAL YEAR OPENS.`

segments.voice: Paper lanterns strung across a temple courtyard. A line of kids pouring scoops of water over a small statue of the baby Buddha. Lamps lit at dusk. That's Vesak, and here's the answer to yesterday's question: in Theravada tradition, one full moon holds three of the Buddha's biggest days, his birth, his awakening and his passing. Some East Asian communities keep the birthday on a day of its own. Either way, this is the fifth time this path has reached it. So we start at the end of the story, under two trees.
screen: `LANTERNS, WATER, LAMPS.` → `BIRTH, AWAKENING, PASSING.` → `THE FIFTH TIME.`

segments.voice: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta tells it. The Buddha, old and ill, reaches Kusinara and lies down on his right side between twin sala trees. Then the trees burst into bloom out of season, and the sutta says their blossoms fall over his body, with flowers and music from the sky as well. A beautiful scene, and the Buddha turns it around. He tells Ananda that this is not how he is truly honored. Whoever lives the Dhamma, practicing it properly, small things and great, that one honors him with the highest honor. Here's the teaching Buddhists draw from that night. There are two kinds of offering: offering things, lamps and flowers and incense, and offering practice. Both are real, and tradition holds the second one higher. It's why Vesak has both: lanterns in the courtyard, and people taking the precepts, some keeping extra ones for the day. So the night comes down to this: the Buddha, dying, under blossoms falling just for him, said the flowers weren't the point. Now look back at this block with that in mind. Few wants, room to breathe, three jewels, your vow, said aloud, a life of practice. None of those is a lamp. All of them are the other offering. Five Vesaks on this path, five years of lamps, and what the lamps stand for is the days in between.
screen: `TWIN SALA TREES AT KUSINARA.` · `BLOSSOMS OUT OF SEASON.` · `NOT HOW HE IS HONORED.` · `TWO OFFERINGS: THINGS, PRACTICE.` · then, large: `FIVE YEARS OF LAMPS.`

segments.voice: If you have candles or tea lights and a safe place, light five, one for each Vesak on this path; if not, set out five small things in a row. As you light or set out each one, name one thing from these years you'll keep doing. Then sit with the five in front of you, and watch the light, or the row, hold still.
Vesak: the full moon of the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing, honored with lamps, and with practice, puja of both kinds.
Take this along: five years of lamps, and the days of practice they stand for. One of seven in the festival year.

screen: `DAY 1771 COUNTS.` → `THE FESTIVAL YEAR · 1 OF 7.` → `TOMORROW: AFTER HE WOKE UP, WHO HEARD HIS FIRST SERMON?`

howItsDone: At Vesak, Buddhists visit temples, light lamps and lanterns, offer flowers, and take the precepts, some keeping extra precepts for the day; in some communities people pour water over a small statue of the baby Buddha.

chat.meaning: Under the sala trees the Buddha said practicing the Dhamma is the highest honor. Lamps are an offering of things; practice is the other kind.

Vesak.meaning: the full-moon festival of the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing

Theravada.meaning: the Buddhism of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia

Mahaparinibbana Sutta.meaning: the sutta of the Buddha's last days and passing

Kusinara.meaning: the town where the Buddha passed away

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta: the twin sala trees and the highest honor)
Vesak observance (Theravada: birth, awakening and passing on one full moon; bathing the Buddha, lamps, precepts)

notes: For parents: the Buddha's death is told gently ('old and ill', 'lies down', 'passing'); no distress described.

DN 16 paraphrased: twin sala trees bloom out of season and drop blossoms on him, with heavenly flowers and music; he tells Ananda this is not how the Tathagata is honored, but by the one who practices the Dhamma properly, in the greater and lesser duties. Confirm the paraphrase.
Amisa puja / patipatti puja named only in the trapdoor as a later teachers' distinction; 'tradition holds the second one higher' rests on DN 16 and that distinction. Confirm.

Vesak as birth, awakening and passing on one full moon is stated for Theravada tradition; East Asian communities keeping the birthday separately is hedged as 'some'. Bathing the baby Buddha is described without naming where. Confirm.
'Fifth time this path has reached it' refers to the app's five-year path (outline hook), not a calendar claim.
Shape: review. Recall carries the block's last six carries (days 1765-1770). Mai's arc: first Vesak with Ông living at home; he asks her to light five lamps.
Surprising fact: dying under blossoms falling just for him, the Buddha said the flowers weren't the point.
Practice adds a flame-safety hedge ('a safe place') and a no-candle option.
